drafted_by: AI, requires clinician review before any real use.

questions.text: What is the main problem: pelvic pain, abnormal bleeding, discharge, missed periods, menopause symptoms, or something else?
questions.rationale: Clarifying the main gynecologic complaint guides the next branch of the interview.

questions.text: When did this start, and is it getting better, worse, or staying the same?
questions.rationale: Onset and course distinguish acute from chronic gynecologic problems.

questions.text: Is pregnancy possible right now, or have you had a positive pregnancy test?
questions.rationale: Pregnancy, including ectopic pregnancy, must be considered with pelvic pain or bleeding.

questions.text: When was your last menstrual period, and was it normal for you?
questions.rationale: Last period dates the cycle and pregnancy risk.

questions.text: Are you bleeding more heavily, spotting between periods, or bleeding after sex or after menopause?
questions.rationale: Pattern of bleeding separates hormonal, structural, pregnancy, and cancer causes.

questions.text: Are you soaking through a pad or tampon every hour, passing large clots, or feeling lightheaded?
questions.rationale: Heavy bleeding with lightheadedness can be hemodynamically important.

questions.text: Where is the pelvic or lower belly pain, and is it one-sided, constant, or crampy?
questions.rationale: Location and quality help separate ovarian, uterine, and gastrointestinal causes.

questions.text: Did the pain start suddenly and become severe on one side?
questions.rationale: Sudden severe unilateral pain raises concern for ovarian torsion or ectopic pregnancy.

questions.text: Do you have vaginal discharge, and what color or odor is it?
questions.rationale: Discharge character helps identify vaginitis, cervicitis, and PID.

questions.text: Any itching, sores, blisters, or pain with sex or urination?
questions.rationale: These features suggest STI, herpes, or local irritation.

questions.text: Have you had fever, chills, or pain with sex along with pelvic pain or discharge?
questions.rationale: Fever with pelvic pain and discharge raises concern for pelvic inflammatory disease.

questions.text: Are your periods regular, and have they stopped, become farther apart, or come more often?
questions.rationale: Cycle change can reflect PCOS, thyroid disease, menopause, or pregnancy.

questions.text: Are you having hot flashes, night sweats, or vaginal dryness, or have your periods stopped?
questions.rationale: Menopausal symptoms are a common primary gynecologic complaint.

questions.text: Are you using contraception, an IUD, or hormone therapy, and has anything changed recently?
questions.rationale: Contraception type changes bleeding, pain, and infection risk.

questions.text: Have you had any new sexual partners or unprotected sex recently?
questions.rationale: Sexual history helps assess STI and pregnancy risk.

questions.text: When was your last Pap or HPV test, and have you had abnormal results?
questions.rationale: Screening history informs cancer risk for bleeding or discharge.

questions.text: Have you had fibroids, endometriosis, ovarian cysts, PID, or gynecologic surgery?
questions.rationale: Prior gynecologic disease often explains recurrent pain or bleeding.

questions.text: Have you had postmenopausal bleeding, a pelvic mass, bloating, or unintended weight loss?
questions.rationale: These features raise concern for gynecologic malignancy.

questions.text: Any burning with urine, leaking, constipation, or pain with bowel movements?
questions.rationale: Urinary and bowel symptoms may be related or point to another system.

questions.text: With the pain or bleeding, have you felt faint, or had pain in your shoulder tip?
questions.rationale: Shoulder-tip pain or syncope with pelvic pain can indicate ruptured ectopic pregnancy.

questions.text: Are you taking blood thinners, hormones, or any new medicines?
questions.rationale: Anticoagulants and hormones commonly change bleeding patterns.

questions.text: Have you had pregnancies, miscarriages, or trouble getting pregnant?
questions.rationale: Obstetric history informs current bleeding and pain workup.

questions.text: How is this affecting work, sex, sleep, or daily activities?
questions.rationale: Functional impact guides urgency and treatment.

questions.text: What is the main thing you are worried this could be?
questions.rationale: Understanding the patient's concern guides reassurance and follow-up questions.

red_flags.label: Possible pregnancy with pain or bleeding
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does the patient report pelvic pain or vaginal bleeding with a possible or positive pregnancy?

red_flags.label: Heavy vaginal bleeding
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does the patient report soaking pads hourly, large clots, or bleeding with lightheadedness?

red_flags.label: Sudden severe one-sided pelvic pain
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does the patient describe sudden severe pain on one side of the pelvis?

red_flags.label: Possible pelvic inflammatory disease
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does the patient report pelvic pain with fever, discharge, or pain with sex?

red_flags.label: Possible ruptured ectopic pregnancy
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does the patient report pelvic pain with fainting or shoulder-tip pain, especially if pregnancy is possible?

red_flags.label: Postmenopausal bleeding or possible cancer features
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does the patient report bleeding after menopause, a pelvic mass, bloating, or weight loss?
